options: VM sprawl expanding the attack surface
q: Dozens of forgotten, unpatched virtual machines remain powered on across a cloud estate. Which risk does this BEST illustrate?

explain: A TPM stores measurements (PCRs) so secure and measured boot can detect unauthorized boot code and support remote attestation. Encryption may use TPM keys but measurement and boot integrity are the primary purpose here.
options: Measured and secure boot to detect tampered boot code
Full disk encryption at rest only
Automatic patching of the operating system
q: During boot, firmware measures each boot component and extends values into a TPM before execution. This process PRIMARILY provides what?

explain: Least privilege requires only the rights needed for assigned duties, for only as long as needed. Standing excess admin rights violate it even if mediation and usability remain intact.
q: A help desk technician is given standing administrator rights just in case they are needed. Which principle is MOST directly violated?

explain: Complete mediation requires checking every access against authority, not relying on a cached or prior decision. Caching without revalidation allows revoked rights to persist.
q: A system caches an authorization decision and stops rechecking it, allowing revoked access to continue. Which principle has failed?

explain: Open design (Kerckhoffs) holds that security must depend only on the secrecy of the key, not on secrecy of the design, so the design can withstand public scrutiny. Obscurity is not a reliable control.
options: Hiding source code at all costs
Secrecy of the design and algorithms
q: Kerckhoffs principle, applied as open design, states that system security should depend on what?

explain: Fail-safe defaults base access on permission rather than exclusion: default deny, allow by explicit exception. Defense in depth is about layering, not the default access decision.
q: A new firewall is deployed with a default-deny rule and access granted only by explicit exception. Which principle is demonstrated?

explain: Economy of mechanism favors simple, small designs that are easier to verify and contain fewer flaws. Simplifying the trusted base directly supports this principle over adding layered complexity.
q: A designer removes unneeded services, simplifies the TCB, and avoids complex mechanisms. Which principle is she applying?

explain: Separation of privilege requires multiple conditions or keys held by different parties so no single person or key suffices. It is related to but distinct from separation of duties in workflows.
q: Releasing a sensitive vault requires both a physical key held by one officer and a code held by another. This BEST illustrates which principle?

explain: Least common mechanism minimizes mechanisms shared by multiple users because shared components can become covert channels or single points of compromise. It is the least applied Saltzer and Schroeder principle on the exam.
q: A shared library used by all users becomes a covert channel risk because all subjects depend on the same mechanism. Which principle warns against this?

explain: Psychological acceptability requires security mechanisms to be usable and not unduly burden users, otherwise users will bypass them. The control may mediate completely yet still fail if people will not use it correctly.
q: Users routinely bypass a security tool because its prompts are confusing and block their work. Which design principle has been neglected?

explain: Layered physical controls exemplify defense in depth: failure of one layer does not expose the asset because independent layers remain. No single control is relied upon alone.
options: Defense in depth through layered controls
q: A facility uses a fence, then badge doors, then a mantrap, then a locked cage for servers. Which concept is BEST demonstrated?

explain: Privacy by design is proactive and preventive: privacy is the default, embedded in design, and maintained end to end. Retrofitting controls or banners alone does not satisfy the principle.
options: Rely solely on user consent banners
Add privacy controls after deployment if complaints arise
Embed privacy proactively, default to privacy, and retain privacy throughout the lifecycle
Collect all data first and minimize later
q: Privacy by design requires which approach to handling personal data?

explain: Under the shared responsibility model for IaaS, the provider secures the physical infrastructure and hypervisor while the customer patches the guest OS, applications, and data. In SaaS that burden shifts to the provider.
options: The end users of the application
q: In an IaaS deployment, who is PRIMARILY responsible for patching the guest operating system?

explain: Even in SaaS, the customer retains responsibility for identities, access management, and its data classification and use. The provider manages application patching and physical facilities.
options: Classifying and handling its own data
Securing the provider physical data center
q: Compared with IaaS, a SaaS customer retains PRIMARY responsibility for which of the following? (Choose two.)

explain: Data residency and sovereignty govern where data is stored and processed and which jurisdiction laws apply. Cloud designs must enforce placement constraints even when the provider operates globally.
q: A regulation requires health data to remain within a specific country. Which cloud concern does this MOST directly raise?

explain: Constrained embedded and IoT devices often cannot host agents or patches, so network segmentation, gateway filtering, and monitoring compensate. Placing them flat or Internet-facing magnifies their weaknesses.
options: Give it direct Internet access for updates
Segment it on an isolated network with monitored gateway controls
Disable all logging for the device
Place it on the flat corporate LAN
q: An IoT sensor cannot run endpoint agents, uses a default password, and cannot be patched in the field. The BEST compensating design is to do what?

explain: ICS and SCADA prioritize availability and human safety, often run legacy systems that cannot be patched or rebooted freely, and require specialized controls. Confidentiality-first office IT assumptions do not transfer.
options: ICS prioritizes availability and safety, runs legacy unpatchable systems, and tolerates little downtime
ICS uses the same patch cadence as office workstations
ICS prioritizes confidentiality above availability and safety
ICS systems are always air-gapped and need no monitoring
q: Which statement BEST captures the primary SCADA and ICS security concern versus office IT?

explain: Fail-safe (fail-open) unlocks on failure to protect life safety, as with egress doors. Fail-secure stays locked on failure to protect assets, as with a vault. Design must choose per door based on safety versus security.
options: Life safety doors fail open (fail-safe) while asset doors fail secure
q: On fire alarm, stairwell doors unlock to allow evacuation while the vault door stays locked. This pairing BEST shows what?

explain: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) uses natural surveillance, access control, and territorial reinforcement to deter offenders. It shapes behavior through the environment rather than electronics alone.
q: Clear sightlines, good lighting, territorial markings, and natural surveillance to deter crime describe which approach?

explain: Site selection weighs natural disasters, local crime, neighboring hazards, utility reliability, and visibility. Locating in a flood plain or under a flight path creates risks no interior control can fully offset.
options: Natural hazards, crime rates, and proximity to hazards such as flood plains and airports
q: When selecting a site for a new data center, which factor should be evaluated FIRST from a security perspective?

explain: A mantrap or access control vestibule traps a single occupant between interlocking doors to verify identity and prevent piggybacking. A simple turnstile counts passage but does not provide the same interlocked verification.
q: A small enclosed vestibule requires the first door to close and identity to verify before the second door opens, preventing tailgating. This is a what?

explain: Bollards are rated barriers that stop or slow vehicles while allowing pedestrian flow. Fences delay people, while bollards specifically address vehicle-borne threats to entrances and storefronts.
q: Short, sturdy posts installed in front of a building entrance to stop a vehicle ramming attack are called what?

explain: A Faraday cage blocks electromagnetic fields and supports TEMPEST controls against eavesdropping on emanations. Ordinary shielding reduces interference but a cage provides full enclosure attenuation.
q: A room is lined with conductive mesh to block electromagnetic emanations from escaping. This control is BEST described as what?

explain: Plenum spaces circulate air, so cables there must be plenum-rated with low smoke and flame toxicity. Non-plenum cable jackets can spread fire and toxic fumes through the HVAC pathway.
options: It must be installed without any labeling
It must be unshielded at all times
It must be plenum-rated so it does not produce toxic smoke in a fire
It must carry both power and data together
q: Cabling run through the air-handling space above a ceiling must meet which requirement?

explain: Low humidity promotes electrostatic discharge, which can damage sensitive electronics. High humidity causes condensation and corrosion. Data centers typically hold roughly 40 to 60 percent relative humidity.
q: A data center keeps relative humidity too low. What risk increases MOST?

explain: Resilience combines dual utility feeds to survive a feed failure and generators with UPS bridging for extended outages. Single strips and removing the UPS reduce resilience.
options: On-site generator with automatic transfer for extended outages
Dual power feeds from separate substations
Removing the UPS to simplify wiring
A single power strip per rack
q: Which combination BEST provides sustained power resilience for a critical facility? (Choose two.)
An attacker floods a web server with SYN packets and never completes the handshake, exhausting the connection backlog. Which defense is MOST effective?
explain: SYN cookies let the server validate handshakes without allocating backlog state for half-open connections — the purpose-built defense against SYN floods. More RAM just delays exhaustion; honeypots detect rather than mitigate; UDP can't carry HTTP.

q: A NIDS alerts on every large file download as "possible exfiltration," overwhelming analysts with benign events. What is this and how should it be tuned?
options: A zero-day; replace the NIDS with an IPS
False negatives; loosen the signature thresholds
False positives; tune the rule to reduce noise
explain: Alerts on benign activity are false positives — an availability/efficiency problem for the SOC. The fix is tuning (refining signatures, adding context/whitelists), not loosening detection broadly (which would create false negatives — missed attacks).

q: A company deploys public web servers where Internet users can reach them but the internal LAN stays isolated. Which architecture is this?
options: A screened subnet (DMZ) between two firewalls
A VPN concentrator on the LAN
explain: A DMZ/screened subnet places public-facing servers in a buffer zone between an external and internal firewall. VLANs alone don't create this isolation; a VPN concentrator serves remote users; air-gapping disconnects entirely.

q: Which Wi-Fi standard should a company deploy for new access points today, and why?
options: WPA2, because WPA3 lacks enterprise support
WPA3, for SAE handshake and forward secrecy
explain: WPA3 is the current best practice (SAE replaces the vulnerable PSK handshake, forward secrecy, stronger encryption; Enterprise mode offers 192-bit security). WEP is broken, WPA2 is the legacy baseline, and MAC filtering/open auth is not real security.

q: Users report being redirected to a perfect replica of the corporate login page after a DNS cache was poisoned. Which control would have prevented the redirection from being trusted?
explain: DNSSEC cryptographically authenticates DNS responses, so poisoned cache entries fail validation. Longer TTLs make poisoning persist longer; split tunneling and IPS signatures don't authenticate DNS data.
Layer 3, Network, provides logical addressing such as IP and routing between networks. Layer 2 uses physical MAC addresses within a local segment, while Layer 4 handles end-to-end transport.
q: Which OSI layer is responsible for logical addressing and routing packets between different networks?

explain: SSH on port 22 encrypts remote shell sessions and replaces insecure Telnet and rlogin. FTP, TFTP, and SNMP serve different purposes and their legacy versions do not provide a secure interactive shell.
q: An administrator needs a secure replacement for Telnet for remote command-line administration. Which protocol and port should be used?

explain: The Physical layer transmits raw bits over the medium. Data Link uses frames, Network uses packets, and Transport uses segments for TCP, which makes bit the only correct choice here.
q: What is the protocol data unit at the OSI Physical layer?

explain: Presentation, Layer 6, translates data formats and handles encryption and compression so applications can understand it. Routing is Layer 3, reliability is Layer 4, and framing is Layer 2.
options: Framing data for the local segment
q: Which function is primarily performed at the OSI Presentation layer?

explain: Traditional switches operate at Layer 2 using MAC addresses to forward frames within a LAN. Routers operate at Layer 3 with packets, while Layer 1 devices merely repeat bits without address awareness.
q: A switch forwards traffic based on MAC addresses. At which OSI layer does a traditional switch primarily operate, and what data unit does it process?

explain: Each layer adds its own control information as a header, wrapping the upper-layer data into a new unit. De-encapsulation on the receiving host reverses this; encryption and address translation are not the definition of encapsulation.
options: Headers are removed and data is encrypted
A header, and sometimes a trailer, is added to the data from the layer above
The data is converted directly into bits with no control information
Logical addresses are replaced with physical addresses
q: During encapsulation as data moves down the OSI stack, what happens at each layer?

explain: The Session layer, Layer 5, controls dialogs, synchronization, and session recovery between applications. Transport provides end-to-end delivery, but session management and checkpointing are Layer 5 functions.
q: Which OSI layer establishes, manages, and terminates dialogs between applications and provides checkpointing?

explain: HTTP, SMTP, and FTP provide services directly to user applications at Layer 7. IP is Layer 3, TCP and UDP are Layer 4, and Ethernet is a Layer 2 technology, so the other lists sit at lower layers.
q: Which list correctly maps example protocols to the OSI Application layer?

explain: The TCP/IP Application layer absorbs OSI Application, Presentation, and Session functions. Data Link and Physical map to TCP/IP Network Access, and OSI Network maps to TCP/IP Internet, not to Application.
options: Session and Presentation, along with Application
q: In the TCP/IP model, which two OSI layers are combined into the TCP/IP Application layer?

explain: De-encapsulation is the receiving-side removal of each layer header in reverse order until the original data reaches the application. Encapsulation is the sending-side addition of headers, the opposite direction.
q: A host receives a frame, strips the Ethernet header, then strips the IP header, then strips the TCP header before delivering data to the application. What process is this?

explain: The initiator sends SYN, the responder replies SYN-ACK, and the initiator confirms with ACK, synchronizing sequence numbers both ways. Any sequence starting with ACK or including FIN does not establish a new connection.
q: Which is the correct sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?

explain: UDP suits real-time voice because low latency matters more than perfect delivery, and retransmitted audio would arrive too late to use. TCP guarantees delivery but its retransmissions and ordering add delay that harms live media.
options: UDP, because it is connectionless with low overhead and no retransmission delay
SCTP, because it encrypts all voice media by default
TCP, because it guarantees delivery of every packet in order
ICMP, because it reports delivery errors to the application
q: A live voice application tolerates occasional packet loss but cannot tolerate retransmission delay and jitter. Which transport protocol is the best fit and why?

explain: UDP is connectionless, offers no delivery guarantee, and uses a small header, giving it lower overhead than TCP. Handshakes, flow control, and congestion control are TCP features, so those options describe the wrong protocol.
options: It has a smaller header and lower overhead than TCP
It is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery
It provides flow control and congestion control
It uses a three-way handshake before sending data
q: Which characteristics are true of UDP? (Choose two.)

explain: DNS uses UDP 53 for most queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and oversized responses. Port 161 is SNMP and port 389 is LDAP, so recognizing both DNS transports matters for a correct rule.
options: UDP 53, with TCP 53 for large responses and zone transfers
q: A service must be identified for a firewall rule. Standard DNS queries primarily use which port?

explain: DHCP clients send from UDP 68 to servers on UDP 67 to obtain address configuration. Reversing the ports is the classic trap; DNS resolves names and TFTP transfers files without access control.
options: DHCP, client port 67 to server port 68
DHCP, client port 68 to server port 67
q: A workstation broadcasts a request to obtain an IP address automatically. Which protocol and ports are involved?

explain: POP3 uses port 110 and IMAP uses port 143 in their standard plaintext forms; the secure variants use 995 and 993. Swapping 110 and 143 is the distractor, and port 25 is SMTP submission and relay territory.
options: POP3 on port 110 and IMAP on port 143
POP3 on port 25 and IMAP on port 110
POP3 on port 993 and IMAP on port 995
POP3 on port 143 and IMAP on port 110
q: Which pairing of email retrieval protocol and default port is correct?

explain: SNMP traps are unsolicited agent notifications sent to the manager on UDP 162, while managers poll agents on UDP 161. NTP uses port 123, so the port number itself distinguishes polling from traps.
options: An SNMP manager polling an agent on its standard port
An SNMP trap notification sent to the manager
A syslog message sent over UDP
q: An engineer sees UDP traffic destined for port 162 at a management station. What is this traffic most likely to be?

explain: LDAPS wraps LDAP in TLS on port 636, encrypting directory traffic that is cleartext on port 389. Kerberos on port 88 provides authentication but does not by itself encrypt LDAP queries.
options: Keep port 389 and enable TFTP on port 69
Move LDAP from port 389 to LDAPS on port 636
Move LDAP to Kerberos on port 88
Move LDAP from port 389 to SNMPv3 on port 161
q: Directory lookups are crossing the network in cleartext and must be encrypted. Which change accomplishes this using the standard secure port?

explain: Port 3389 is Remote Desktop Protocol, and internet-exposed RDP is heavily targeted for password attacks and exploitation. SSH uses port 22 and Telnet uses port 23, so the port identifies RDP unambiguously.
options: VNC; it transmits all traffic in cleartext by default
SSH; it allows unauthenticated file transfer
Telnet; it has no authentication mechanism
RDP; it becomes a high-value brute-force and credential attack target
q: A help desk tool connects to Windows hosts on TCP port 3389. Which service is being used, and what is the main security concern if it is exposed to the internet?

explain: NTP on UDP 123 synchronizes clocks, and Kerberos tolerates only small clock skew before rejecting tickets, while forensic log correlation depends on aligned timestamps. The other protocols resolve names, manage devices, or assign addresses.
q: Accurate, synchronized time is required so that Kerberos authentication and log correlation work correctly. Which protocol and port provide this?

explain: SIP uses port 5060 for unencrypted signaling and port 5061 when protected with TLS. Choosing 5060 leaves signaling in cleartext, and port 3389 belongs to RDP, not voice signaling.
options: 5060 over UDP only, because SIP cannot use TLS
q: A VoIP phone registers using SIP over TLS. Which port should be expected for the signaling traffic?

explain: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 is private, so 172.20.14.9 qualifies, as do 10.0.0.0/8 and 192.168.0.0/16. The 169.254 range is link-local APIPA, not RFC 1918, and the others are public addresses.
q: Which of the following addresses falls within an RFC 1918 private IPv4 range?

explain: Port Address Translation multiplexes many internal hosts onto a single public address by tracking distinct source ports. Static NAT is one-to-one and would exhaust addresses, which is exactly the problem PAT solves.
options: DNSSEC, signing records so hosts can share an address securely
DHCP relay, forwarding address requests to an external server
PAT, translating many internal addresses to one public address using distinct source ports
Static NAT, mapping each internal host to a dedicated public address
q: An organization with one public IP address needs hundreds of internal hosts to reach the internet simultaneously. Which technology provides this, and how?

explain: NAT alters addresses and ports, breaking the end-to-end model and conflicting with protocols that embed addresses in payloads or integrity-protect headers, notably IPsec AH. NAT does not encrypt traffic or force IPv6 use.
options: It encrypts traffic in a way endpoints cannot decrypt
It prevents all use of private addressing internally
It forces all hosts to use IPv6 addresses
It breaks end-to-end connectivity and complicates protocols that embed addresses or require integrity checks, such as IPsec AH
q: What is a recognized drawback of relying heavily on NAT in a network design?

explain: IPv6 expands addresses to 128 bits and eliminates broadcast, using multicast and anycast instead. It was designed to reduce dependence on NAT, and confusing it with 64-bit addressing or broadcast understates its core changes.
options: IPv6 addresses are 64 bits to keep headers small
IPv6 requires NAT to reach the internet
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and uses multicast and anycast instead of broadcast
IPv6 relies on broadcast for neighbor discovery
q: Which statement about IPv6 is correct?

explain: Transition tunneling encapsulates IPv6 packets inside IPv4 so they can cross IPv4-only networks. Dual stack runs both protocols natively on hosts rather than encapsulating one inside the other.
options: Anycasting IPv4 addresses to IPv6 routers
Tunneling, encapsulating IPv6 inside IPv4 for transit
NAT64 translating all IPv4 addresses to private ranges
q: During IPv6 migration, an organization carries IPv6 packets across an existing IPv4-only infrastructure. Which concept describes this approach?

explain: Early IPv6 specifications mandated IPsec, and current standards make it integrated and recommended rather than strictly mandatory. IPv6 does not forbid IPsec or replace network-layer protection with TLS, which operates above the transport layer.
options: IPv6 requires AH but prohibits ESP
IPsec was originally mandatory in IPv6 specifications and is now an integrated, recommended capability rather than a strict requirement
IPv6 replaces IPsec entirely with TLS at the network layer
IPsec support is forbidden in IPv6 to improve speed
q: Which statement best reflects the current status of IPsec in IPv6?

explain: Every SSL version is deprecated due to known vulnerabilities, and modern services should require TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. A valid certificate does not fix protocol-level flaws in SSL, and SSL and TLS are not interchangeable.
options: SSL 3.0 is stronger than TLS 1.2 because it is older and proven
SSL 3.0 is acceptable if the certificate is valid
TLS and SSL are interchangeable names for the same protocol
All SSL versions are deprecated; TLS 1.2 or preferably TLS 1.3 should be required
q: A web service still negotiates SSL 3.0 with some clients. What is the correct security position?

explain: The TLS handshake negotiates algorithms, authenticates the server and optionally the client with certificates, and derives session keys for encrypted data. Application data is not sent in cleartext as part of that negotiation.
options: The server compresses all application data for the session
Both peers exchange application data in cleartext to agree on a language
The client downloads the server certificate revocation list for the year
Peers negotiate cipher suites, authenticate using certificates, and establish shared session keys
q: What is accomplished during the TLS handshake before application data flows?

explain: TLS 1.3 drops legacy algorithms, mandates ephemeral key exchange for forward secrecy, and reduces handshake round trips. Restoring static RSA or weak ciphers would reverse its security goals, not define it.
options: It eliminates certificates in favor of pre-shared passwords only
It moves encryption from the transport area to the network layer
It restores support for static RSA key exchange and weak ciphers
It removes obsolete cryptography, requires forward secrecy with ephemeral key exchange, and shortens the handshake
q: Which improvement is a defining feature of TLS 1.3 compared with earlier versions?

explain: SFTP is a distinct file transfer protocol built on SSH, whereas FTPS adds TLS to the original FTP protocol with separate control and data channels. Swapping the two descriptions is the classic exam trap.
options: SFTP runs over SSH as a separate protocol, while FTPS is FTP secured with TLS
They are the same protocol with two names
FTPS runs over SSH, while SFTP is FTP secured with TLS
q: Which statement correctly distinguishes SFTP from FTPS?

explain: Implicit FTPS uses port 990 for control and port 989 for data, with TLS established immediately on connection. Port 22 is SSH and SFTP, and explicit FTPS starts on the standard FTP ports before upgrading with TLS.
options: Control on port 22 and data on port 20
Control on port 990 and data on port 989
Control on port 69 and data on port 68
Control on port 443 and data on port 80
q: A partner insists on FTPS in implicit mode. Which ports should the security engineer expect?

explain: AH provides integrity and authentication of packets without encrypting the payload, exactly matching the requirement. ESP is the IPsec protocol that provides confidentiality, so selecting ESP misses the no-encryption condition.
q: An IPsec requirement calls for data origin authentication and integrity but explicitly no confidentiality, because encryption is handled elsewhere. Which IPsec protocol fits?

explain: ESP encrypts the payload for confidentiality and can also provide integrity and authentication, while AH provides no encryption at all. Key management is handled by IKE, not by ESP itself.
options: Confidentiality through encryption of the payload
Integrity checking of the IP header
q: Which services does IPsec ESP provide that AH does not?

explain: Tunnel mode encrypts and encapsulates the entire original packet inside a new IP header, which is the standard gateway-to-gateway design. Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original header in place for end-to-end host use.
q: Two branch-office gateways protect all traffic between sites so that internal host addresses are hidden and the entire original packet is protected. Which IPsec mode is in use?

explain: ESP provides confidentiality via encryption and, when configured, integrity and authentication of the protected data. It operates at the network layer and provides neither reliable delivery like TCP nor name resolution like DNS.
options: Integrity and data origin authentication when authentication is enabled
Automatic DNS name resolution for both peers
q: Which features are provided by IPsec ESP? (Choose two.)

explain: IKE authenticates peers and negotiates the security associations and keys that AH and ESP then use to protect traffic, using ISAKMP for the framework and Oakley for key exchange. IKE itself does not encrypt the user data stream.
options: It negotiates security associations and exchanges keying material, building on ISAKMP and Oakley concepts
It assigns IP addresses to remote clients like DHCP
It replaces ESP and AH as the data protection protocol
It encrypts application data directly at Layer 7
q: What is the role of IKE in an IPsec deployment?

explain: A security association is unidirectional and uniquely identified by destination address, protocol, and SPI, so two-way traffic needs two associations. Treating one association as bidirectional is the trap the question tests.
options: A single association protects traffic equally in both directions
Associations are unidirectional, so a bidirectional exchange typically needs a pair, each identified in part by a Security Parameter Index
Associations are negotiated by DNSSEC before IKE runs
An association is the same thing as a TLS session ticket
q: Which statement about IPsec security associations is correct?

explain: AH computes integrity over immutable header fields including the source address, so when NAT rewrites that address the check fails at the receiver. ESP does not protect the outer header the same way, which is why AH and NAT conflict.
options: NAT converts IPv4 packets to IPv6 which AH cannot process
AH requires UDP port 500 which NAT always blocks
AH encrypts the payload so NAT cannot read port numbers
AH integrity-protects the IP header including source address, so NAT address changes invalidate the integrity check
q: Why does NAT commonly break IPsec AH-protected traffic?

explain: DNSSEC signs record sets so resolvers can verify origin authenticity and that data was not altered in transit. It does not encrypt queries, so confidentiality claims describe DoT or DoH instead of DNSSEC.
options: Confidentiality by encrypting all DNS queries
Authenticity and integrity through digitally signed record sets
q: What security does DNSSEC provide for DNS responses?

explain: DoT and DoH both encrypt the client-to-resolver channel, protecting query confidentiality. DNSSEC only signs data for authenticity and does not encrypt, and changing TTLs affects caching, not confidentiality.
options: DNSSEC alone, because signing encrypts the query
Increasing the DNS TTL so queries are sent less often
DNS over TLS, encrypting queries to the resolver
DNS over HTTPS, carrying queries inside HTTPS
q: An organization wants to encrypt DNS queries between clients and the resolver to prevent on-path eavesdropping, without changing what DNS data is returned. Which options fit this goal? (Choose two.)

explain: Base DNS lacks authentication of responses, enabling cache poisoning with forged answers that resolvers accept. DNSSEC addresses this directly with cryptographic signatures that resolvers validate before caching.
options: DNS uses TCP only; switching to UDP mitigates it
DNS has no built-in response authentication in its base design; DNSSEC mitigates it with signed records
DNS compresses responses; disabling compression mitigates it
DNS encrypts responses with the wrong key; longer TTLs mitigate it
q: A resolver accepts spoofed responses because it cannot verify that answers truly came from the authoritative source. Which protocol-level weakness is being exploited, and what mitigates it?

explain: S/MIME is built on hierarchical PKI with X.509 certificates issued by certificate authorities, while PGP grew around users signing each others keys in a web of trust. Both can encrypt and sign, so the difference is the trust model.
options: PGP requires X.509 certificates, while S/MIME uses a web of trust
Neither provides encryption, only digital signatures
S/MIME uses X.509 certificates from a PKI hierarchy, while PGP traditionally uses a decentralized web of trust
Both rely exclusively on a central certificate authority hierarchy
q: Which statement best contrasts the trust models of S/MIME and PGP for secure email?

explain: SPF publishes authorized sending hosts in DNS so receivers can verify the connecting IP against the envelope sender domain. DKIM instead verifies a cryptographic signature, and DMARC builds policy on top of both results.
q: A receiving mail server checks whether the sending server IP address is authorized to send mail for the sender domain by consulting a DNS record. Which mechanism is this?

explain: DKIM signs outbound mail with the domain private key and publishes the public key in DNS, letting receivers verify the signature and detect alteration. SPF checks sending IPs and has no per-message signature, which rules it out.
q: An investigator verifies a cryptographic signature in a message header that was created with a private key whose public key is published in DNS by the sending domain. Which mechanism produced this evidence?

explain: DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail to align with the visible From domain and requests aggregate and forensic reports. SPF and DKIM alone provide checks but no unified policy or reporting mechanism.
options: An SPF record with a hard fail qualifier only
A DKIM selector with a longer key
A DMARC record, which sets policy and reporting based on SPF and DKIM alignment
An MX record pointing to a reporting server
q: A domain owner wants receivers to reject mail that fails alignment checks and wants aggregate reports about who is sending mail claiming to be the domain. Which record should be published?

explain: SRTP encrypts and authenticates the real-time media stream carrying the actual voice. SIP and H.323 are primarily signaling protocols that set up calls and do not by themselves encrypt the media path.
q: VoIP calls are being eavesdropped on because the media stream itself is unprotected, even though call setup is secured. Which protocol protects the voice media?

explain: SIP and H.323 are the classic VoIP signaling standards for establishing and controlling calls. SRTP protects media rather than signaling it, and TLS and IPsec are general security protocols, not VoIP signaling standards.
q: Which pairing correctly identifies VoIP signaling protocols?

explain: iSCSI encapsulates SCSI block commands in TCP/IP so storage traffic runs over ordinary IP networks. FCoE maps Fibre Channel onto Ethernet instead, and MPLS is a forwarding mechanism, not a storage protocol.
options: FCoE only, because iSCSI requires dedicated fiber
MPLS, which labels storage frames for switching
SRTP, which encrypts storage blocks in transit
iSCSI, which carries SCSI commands over TCP/IP networks
q: A storage team wants block-level storage access carried over the existing IP network using standard Ethernet infrastructure. Which converged protocol fits?

explain: MPLS forwards traffic using labels assigned to predetermined paths, enabling fast switching and traffic engineering such as provider VPN services. MPLS does not encrypt traffic by default, a frequent misconception the distractors exploit.
options: To provide block storage to converged networks
To forward packets quickly using short labels and predetermined paths rather than longest-prefix IP lookups
To replace DNS with label-based name resolution
To encrypt all customer traffic by default
q: What is the primary purpose of MPLS in a provider network?

explain: A CDN caches and serves content from geographically distributed edge servers near users, cutting latency and origin load. A forward proxy serves a local client population but does not distribute the origin content worldwide.
options: A content delivery network, or CDN
A forward proxy at each user site
q: A global website places copies of static content on servers close to users so pages load faster and origin load drops. What is this service?

explain: Hubs repeat all traffic out every port, creating one collision domain and exposing frames to all hosts. Switches forward only to the needed port using a MAC table, improving both performance and traffic isolation without encrypting anything.
options: A switch assigns IP addresses so frames no longer collide
A switch encrypts every frame before forwarding it
A switch compresses frames to half their original size
A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the destination port, while a hub repeats all traffic to every port
q: Why does replacing a hub with a switch improve LAN performance and reduce unnecessary exposure of traffic?

explain: A forward proxy represents outbound clients fetching external content, while a reverse proxy represents inbound requests to protected servers, enabling caching, load distribution, and shielding. Swapping the labels is the standard confusion.
options: The user-facing one is a reverse proxy and the server-facing one is a forward proxy
The user-facing one is a forward proxy and the server-facing one is a reverse proxy
q: An organization deploys one proxy to fetch external websites on behalf of internal users, and another in front of its public web servers to handle incoming client requests. What are these roles called?

explain: Load balancers spread requests across a server pool so no single server is overwhelmed and the service survives a server failure. Protocol translation is a gateway role, and address assignment belongs to DHCP.
options: To sign DNS records for the application domain
To distribute incoming requests across multiple servers for scalability and availability
To translate between two incompatible network protocols
To assign IP addresses to new servers automatically
q: What is the primary function of a load balancer in front of a web application tier?

explain: A gateway translates between dissimilar protocols, architectures, or formats, operating across layers as needed. Repeaters only regenerate signals, hubs repeat traffic, and bridges connect similar LAN segments at Layer 2.
q: Two systems using different protocol stacks and data formats must exchange information, and a dedicated device is placed between them to translate. What is this device called?

explain: Scope grows from PAN for personal-area links, to LAN for a site, to MAN for a metropolitan area such as a campus city footprint, to WAN across regions. The distractors deliberately assign examples to scopes that are far too large or small.
options: A campus spanning several buildings in one city area is a MAN, and a single office floor is a LAN
A connection between offices on different continents is a PAN
A Bluetooth headset link is a WAN
A home network and the global internet are both LANs
q: Which classification correctly matches network scope to example?

explain: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path before communication begins, as in traditional telephony, while packet switching breaks data into packets routed independently over shared links. The guarantees described in the distractors reverse the two models.
options: Circuit switching shares one path among all users with no setup
Circuit switching dedicates an end-to-end path for the duration of a communication, while packet switching forwards discrete packets that may take different routes
Circuit switching is used only for email, and packet switching only for voice
Packet switching guarantees a fixed bandwidth path for each call
q: How does circuit switching differ from packet switching?

explain: SDN separates decision-making into a centralized control plane that programs forwarding behavior from the data plane that moves packets on devices. Reversing them misstates the architecture that gives SDN its programmability.
options: Both planes exist only inside the application being served
The control plane forwards packets and the data plane makes routing decisions
The control plane is the physical cabling and the data plane is the documentation
The control plane makes centralized decisions about where traffic goes, while the data plane on switches actually forwards traffic
q: In a software-defined network, what is the role of the control plane compared with the data plane?

explain: Fiber uses light, making it immune to EMI and capable of long distances with low signal loss. Fiber does not carry electrical signals, and undetected tapping is actually harder on fiber than on copper, not easier.
options: It can be tapped easily without detection
Much longer transmission distances with lower attenuation
It carries electrical signals that power end devices
q: Which advantages does fiber-optic cabling offer over copper? (Choose two.)

explain: Single-mode fiber uses a very narrow core so light travels in one path, enabling multi-kilometer, high-bandwidth links. Multimode suffers modal dispersion over distance, and copper twisted pair is limited to about 100 meters per run.
options: Coaxial cable, because fiber cannot leave a building
Multimode fiber, because its wide core is designed for the longest distances
Category 5e twisted pair, because it is rated for multi-kilometer runs
Single-mode fiber, because its narrow core supports long distances with minimal modal dispersion
q: A link must span several kilometers between buildings. Which fiber type is appropriate, and why?

explain: Nearby electrical equipment induces EMI and crosstalk on copper, and twisted-pair design with balanced twisting, and shielding in shielded variants, counters it. Modal dispersion is a fiber phenomenon, and cable categories do not amplify signals.
options: Modal dispersion in the copper core
Jitter caused by the speed of light in copper
Attenuation alone; higher categories amplify the signal
Electromagnetic interference and crosstalk; shielding and proper twisting in twisted-pair cable reduce these effects
q: Users near heavy electrical equipment report errors on copper runs. Which transmission impairment and cable property are most relevant?

explain: Baseband dedicates the full bandwidth of the medium to a single digital signal, as in most Ethernet, while broadband splits the medium into channels carrying multiple signals, as in cable television systems. The distractors reverse or misassign the media.
options: Broadband sends one signal and baseband sends many signals at once
Baseband requires fiber and broadband requires copper
Baseband uses the entire medium for one digital signal, while broadband divides the medium into multiple frequency channels
Baseband is always wireless and broadband is always wired
q: What is the difference between baseband and broadband transmission?

explain: SNMPv1 and v2c send community strings and management data in cleartext, exposing credentials and device information to sniffing. SNMPv3 fixes this with authentication and encryption, which is why it is the secure replacement.
options: SNMPv2c uses port 3389 which conflicts with RDP
SNMPv2c requires certificates that expire every day
SNMPv2c encrypts too strongly for older managers to read
Community strings act as passwords and are sent in cleartext, and v2c provides no encryption of management data
q: A legacy deployment still uses SNMPv2c with community strings to manage network devices. What is the core security problem?

explain: TFTP on UDP 69 provides no authentication and no confidentiality, making exposed TFTP services a classic way to steal or tamper with device configurations. Its simplicity is the risk, not obsolete encryption or Kerberos requirements.
options: TFTP only works over IPv6 which the network does not support
TFTP encrypts files with an obsolete cipher that is slow to crack
TFTP requires Kerberos tickets that are hard to manage
TFTP has no authentication and no encryption, so anyone who can reach it may read or overwrite files
q: Engineers use TFTP to push configuration files because it is simple, but a review flags it as risky. Why?

explain: Kerberos authenticates with tickets issued by the Key Distribution Center using symmetric cryptography, avoiding password transmission, but ticket lifetimes make it sensitive to clock skew. It is an authentication protocol, not file transfer or name resolution.
options: Kerberos uses tickets and symmetric cryptography so passwords are not sent over the network, and it depends on synchronized clocks
Kerberos sends user passwords in cleartext to the KDC
Kerberos provides DNS resolution for authentication servers
Kerberos is a file transfer protocol that replaces SFTP
q: Which statement about Kerberos traffic on port 88 is most accurate for a network security review?

explain: Transport mode protects the payload end-to-end between hosts while leaving the original IP header in place, which matches the stated need. Tunnel mode adds a new outer header and is designed for gateway-to-gateway protection of whole packets.
q: A design must protect a host-to-host management session where the original IP header must remain visible for routing and only the payload needs protection. Which IPsec combination fits?

explain: FTP transmits usernames, passwords, and file data in cleartext on ports 20 and 21, so any on-path observer can capture credentials. SFTP or FTPS provide encrypted alternatives, while plain FTP offers no confidentiality despite its popularity.
options: FTP uses port 22 and is identical to SSH
FTP sends credentials and data in cleartext
FTP requires multifactor authentication by default
FTP encrypts credentials but not file data
q: Why is plain FTP considered insecure for transferring sensitive files across an untrusted network?

explain: IPv6 provides a much larger 128-bit address space and integrated support for IPsec as a standard capability. It does not rely on broadcast, and address shortage relief is a design goal rather than a continued limitation.
options: It keeps the IPv4 limit of about four billion addresses
It relies on broadcast for host discovery
IPsec support is integrated into the protocol suite
It provides a vastly larger 128-bit address space
q: Which statements about IPv6 are correct? (Choose two.)
What is the default action of a properly configured firewall rule base when no rule matches a packet?
options: Return the traffic to the sender uninspected
Forward the traffic to the DMZ
explain: Implicit deny means unmatched traffic is dropped by default. Allowing unmatched traffic defeats the rule base, forwarding it to the DMZ still exposes a system, and returning it uninspected is not a firewall function.

q: A security appliance observes copies of traffic from a span port and sends alerts but cannot block traffic. What is this system?
explain: An IDS monitors and alerts but does not sit inline to block traffic. An IPS is inline and can drop malicious traffic, a WAF filters web application requests, and a firewall enforces access rules.

q: What is the primary purpose of placing a public web server in a DMZ?
options: To hide internal IP addresses only
To isolate it from the internal network while allowing public access
explain: A DMZ isolates publicly accessible systems so a compromise does not give direct access to the internal network. It does not itself encrypt traffic, add bandwidth, or serve only as address hiding.

q: An organization uses only a stateless packet filter at its perimeter. What important capability does this firewall lack?
options: Tracking connection state to validate return traffic
explain: A stateless filter judges each packet alone and cannot validate it against an established session. It can still filter by port, address, and protocol, which makes state tracking its key gap.

q: A stateful inspection firewall permits return traffic for an outbound session without a separate inbound rule. Why can it do this safely?
options: It maintains a state table of established connections
It disables logging for return traffic
explain: The state table records established sessions, so matching return traffic is allowed as part of a known connection. Stateful inspection does not require decryption, full proxying, or disabling logs.

q: Which firewall type terminates the client connection and creates a new connection to the server on behalf of the client?
explain: An application proxy terminates one connection and originates another, inspecting application commands. A circuit-level proxy is more generic and session-based, while packet filters and stateful inspectors do not act as endpoints.

q: A firewall administrator places a broad allow rule above a specific deny rule for the same server, and the deny rule never triggers. What principle explains this?
explain: Most rule bases evaluate top down and act on the first match, so the broad allow wins. Implicit deny applies only when nothing matches, and the issue is ordering rather than failure mode or egress policy.

q: What best describes a bastion host?
options: A hardened system intentionally exposed to untrusted networks
An internal file server left with default settings
A wireless controller in the data center
explain: A bastion host is hardened, minimized, and monitored because it is deliberately placed where untrusted traffic can reach it. Ordinary internal servers and controllers are not built for that exposure.

q: Why should an organization apply egress filtering at its perimeter in addition to ingress filtering?
options: To replace the need for patching
To allow all outbound traffic by default
To stop compromised internal hosts from sending spam or attacking others
To eliminate the need for NAT
explain: Egress filtering restricts outbound traffic to approved services, limiting spam, botnet command channels, and data leaks from compromised hosts. It does not replace patching or remove the need for NAT.

q: A company faces SQL injection attempts against its customer portal. Which control is MOST specifically designed to inspect and block this traffic?
explain: A WAF inspects HTTP traffic and application inputs to block attacks such as SQL injection. A packet filter lacks application context, a concentrator handles tunnels, and a monitor-only IDS only alerts.

q: What capability most clearly distinguishes a next-generation firewall from a traditional stateful firewall?
options: Use of an implicit deny rule
Application awareness and integrated intrusion prevention
explain: NGFWs add application and user awareness, deep inspection, and integrated IPS functions beyond port and state filtering. Traditional firewalls already filter ports, use implicit deny, and route traffic.

q: In a screened subnet architecture, where are publicly accessible servers placed?
options: Between the external and internal firewalls
On a wireless guest network only
On the trusted LAN with internal workstations
explain: The screened subnet sits between two firewalls so public systems are separated from both the Internet and the internal network. Putting them on the LAN or outside controls removes that layered isolation.

q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of deploying a honeypot in a production network?
options: To attract attackers and generate detection and intelligence
To store backup copies of production data
explain: Any interaction with a honeypot is suspicious by design, making it valuable for early detection and attacker intelligence. It serves no legitimate users and is not a firewall or backup system.

q: An IDS that alerts when traffic patterns deviate from an established baseline of normal behavior is using which detection method?
explain: Anomaly-based detection compares activity to a learned baseline; behavior-based detection similarly profiles expected user and system actions. Signature-based detection instead matches known attack patterns.

q: Which TWO statements correctly describe an intrusion prevention system compared with an intrusion detection system? (Choose two.)
options: It sits inline with the traffic path
It only receives a copy of traffic from a span port
It can drop malicious packets in real time
explain: An IPS is deployed inline and can block or drop malicious traffic in real time. Receiving only a traffic copy describes an IDS, and no detection system is free of false positives.

q: Two branch offices need their networks connected securely over the Internet as if they were on one private network. Which solution BEST fits this need?
options: A remote-access VPN installed separately for each user
A site-to-site VPN between the office gateways
Split tunneling to a cloud service
Open Wi-Fi with a captive portal
explain: A site-to-site VPN connects networks through gateways so hosts communicate without individual clients. Remote-access VPN serves individual users, and neither split tunneling nor open Wi-Fi connects the offices.

q: What is the main security risk of split tunneling on a remote-access VPN?
options: The client can reach the Internet directly while connected to the corporate network
Headquarters cannot route any traffic at all
The tunnel uses too much encryption
explain: Split tunneling lets a client reach untrusted networks and the corporate network at once, creating a bridge for attacks. A full tunnel instead routes all client traffic through the VPN gateway for inspection.

q: Which improvement does WPA3 provide over WPA2-Personal for passphrase-based wireless access?
options: It uses SAE to resist offline dictionary attacks
It removes encryption to improve speed
It shares one open key with all users
explain: WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, resisting offline dictionary attacks on captured handshakes. WPA2 relies on AES-CCMP, which is sound, but its passphrase handshake remains easier to attack offline.

q: In 802.1X, which component is the switch or wireless access point that blocks or allows network access for a connecting device?
explain: The authenticator, typically a switch or access point, enforces access and relays authentication. The supplicant is the client software, and the authentication server validates credentials.

q: An attacker copies contacts and files from a Bluetooth phone without the knowledge of the owner. What is this attack called?
explain: Bluesnarfing is unauthorized data theft over Bluetooth. Bluejacking only sends unsolicited messages, an evil twin is a rogue wireless network, and pharming redirects users through DNS manipulation.

q: During an active exploit, a team discovers its IPS was deployed on a span port in monitor-only mode. What is the MOST accurate assessment of this deployment?
options: The IPS could alert but could not block the traffic
Monitor mode provides stronger blocking than inline mode
The span port converted the IPS into a firewall
The IPS blocked the exploit but failed to log it
explain: A monitor-only device sees a copy of traffic and can alert, but it cannot drop packets passing on the real path. Inline placement is required for prevention, and a span port grants no blocking power.

q: A security team tunes an anomaly-based IDS and alert volume falls sharply, but a later review finds real attacks were missed. What tradeoff occurred?
options: Encryption was disabled on the network
False negatives increased as sensitivity was reduced
explain: Reducing sensitivity lowers noisy false positives but raises false negatives, where real attacks pass without alerts. The missed attacks are the defining cost of over-tuning in that direction.

q: A retailer must allow customers to reach web servers in a DMZ while preventing Internet hosts from initiating connections to internal systems. Which design BEST meets this need?
options: Disabling firewall logging on the DMZ
A stateful firewall permitting only established return traffic inward from the DMZ
A packet filter allowing all inbound traffic to the LAN
Placing the web servers directly on the internal LAN
explain: Stateful enforcement allows solicited responses while blocking unsolicited inbound connections, and the DMZ isolates public servers. Allowing all inbound traffic or LAN placement exposes internal systems directly.

q: Administrators currently log in to production servers directly from their workstations across multiple VLANs. Which change BEST reduces this exposure?
options: Open management ports to the Internet for convenience
Require administration through a hardened jump server in a management zone
Give administrators shared local accounts on each server
Disable multifactor authentication on the servers
explain: A single hardened jump server concentrates, authenticates, and logs administrative access, shrinking the attack surface. Shared accounts, Internet-exposed management, and weaker authentication all increase risk.

q: Attackers who compromise one application server often move laterally to other servers in the same data center. Which control MOST directly limits this east-west movement?
explain: Microsegmentation enforces policy between individual workloads, limiting lateral east-west movement after a compromise. A perimeter firewall mainly controls north-south traffic entering and leaving.

q: A firm adopts zero trust for application access. Which practice BEST reflects that model?
options: Trust all devices once they are on the office LAN
Rely solely on a strong perimeter firewall
Verify identity and device context for every application request
explain: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust from network location and verifies identity, device, and context per request. LAN-based trust and perimeter-only reliance are the older model it replaces.

q: Remote users need access to a single web application from unmanaged kiosk computers where installing a client is impossible. Which option BEST fits?
options: A dedicated leased line to each kiosk
explain: An SSL/TLS VPN portal provides clientless browser access to specific applications, ideal for unmanaged endpoints. IPsec site-to-site serves networks, and unencrypted L2TP exposes credentials and data.

q: Why is L2TP commonly paired with IPsec in remote-access designs?
options: IPsec provides the tunneling that L2TP lacks
L2TP provides strong encryption by itself
IPsec provides the confidentiality and integrity that L2TP lacks
The pairing eliminates the need for authentication
explain: L2TP creates the tunnel but provides no encryption, so IPsec supplies confidentiality and integrity. Authentication is still required, and the roles of the two protocols are not reversed.

q: Laptops frequently join untrusted hotel networks before users remember to start the VPN. Which policy BEST closes this gap?
options: Allow split tunneling to local printers only
Deploy an always-on VPN that connects before user logon
Disable the host firewall while traveling
Rely on users to avoid sensitive sites while traveling
explain: An always-on VPN establishes the protected tunnel automatically, removing reliance on user action on untrusted networks. Advice, split tunneling, and disabling host defenses leave the exposure in place.

q: A company wants each employee to authenticate with individual credentials and to revoke access instantly when someone leaves. Which wireless mode should it deploy?
options: An open network with MAC filtering only
explain: Enterprise mode with 802.1X gives per-user authentication and immediate revocation through the identity store. A shared passphrase cannot be revoked for one person, and WEP and MAC filtering are weak.

q: Which EAP method is considered the strongest for enterprise wireless authentication when a PKI is available?
explain: EAP-TLS uses mutual certificate authentication for both client and server, providing the strongest protection. LEAP and EAP-MD5 rely on weak challenge mechanisms vulnerable to password attacks.

q: Staff report a new open wireless network using the company name near the office, and users have connected to it. What should the security team do FIRST?
options: Treat it as a suspected evil twin, investigate, and warn users to disconnect
Ignore it because open networks are harmless
Change the corporate SSID and take no other action
Upgrade all laptops to WPA3 immediately
explain: An impersonating open network is a classic evil twin, often paired with social engineering lures to intercept traffic, so investigation and immediate user warning come first. Renaming the SSID does not address the active threat.

q: Why should Wi-Fi Protected Setup PIN mode be disabled on routers?
options: The PIN design allows practical brute-force recovery of the network key
The PIN is transmitted in clear text on all networks
The PIN expires too quickly for legitimate use
explain: The WPS PIN validation flaw lets attackers brute-force the PIN in two halves and recover the passphrase. The issue is guessing efficiency, not clear-text broadcast or disabled encryption.

q: Which TWO controls BEST reduce the risk from rogue access points in an office environment? (Choose two.)
options: Wireless intrusion detection to locate unauthorized radios
802.1X port authentication on wired switch ports
explain: Wireless IDS detects and locates rogue radios, and 802.1X on wired ports prevents an unauthorized access point from granting network access. Publishing the passphrase and disabling monitoring increase exposure.

q: A public server is overwhelmed by half-open TCP connections that never complete the handshake. Which defense MOST directly addresses this SYN flood?
options: SYN cookies or rate limiting at the edge
explain: SYN cookies and rate limiting stop half-open requests from exhausting the connection table, unlike defenses for UDP floods, which target connectionless volume. Passwords, DNS controls, and disk encryption do not help.

q: Attackers send small DNS queries with a spoofed victim address to open resolvers, which return much larger responses to the victim. What type of attack is this?
explain: Reflection sends responses to a spoofed victim, and amplification makes each response far larger than the request, multiplying bandwidth. The other attacks target sessions, local caches, or switch segmentation.

q: On a switched LAN, users are being redirected through the machine of an attacker after ARP tables are corrupted. Which switch feature MOST directly prevents this?
explain: Dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP messages against trusted bindings and drops forged replies that poison caches. Mirroring, spanning tree, and QoS do not authenticate ARP traffic.

q: Customers typing the correct bank URL are silently reaching a fraudulent site after an ISP resolver cache was corrupted. Which defense BEST prevents recurrence?
options: Disabling HTTPS on the bank site
explain: DNSSEC lets resolvers validate authentic DNS answers, defeating cache poisoning that drives pharming. Typosquatting exploits misspelled domains instead, and lease length or disabling HTTPS do not protect resolver data.

q: An attacker captures a valid authentication exchange and retransmits it later to gain access. Which mechanism BEST defeats this replay attack?
options: Nonces and timestamps within an authenticated session
explain: Nonces and timestamps make each exchange unique and time-bound, so a captured replay is rejected. Static reusable credentials are exactly what replay exploits, and packet size or logging changes do not help.

q: An attacker on a user VLAN reaches a restricted VLAN by exploiting trunk negotiation on an access port. Which configuration change BEST stops this VLAN hopping?
options: Enable dynamic trunking on all ports
Allow all VLANs on every trunk
Disable DTP and hard-code ports as access with an explicit VLAN
explain: Hard-coding access ports, disabling dynamic trunk negotiation, and port security prevent a host from negotiating a trunk or spoofing devices to reach other VLANs. Trunking everywhere or using VLAN 1 widens exposure.

q: Employees use a legacy hub segment where any attached device can read all traffic. What is the MOST effective immediate protection for sensitive data crossing that segment?
options: Encrypting traffic end to end with TLS or IPsec
explain: On shared media every station sees all frames, so end-to-end encryption is what protects content from eavesdropping. Renaming, speed, and share visibility do nothing against packet capture.

q: Logs show one external host sequentially probing hundreds of ports on a server within a minute, receiving mostly closed responses. How should this activity be classified?
explain: Rapid sequential probing of many ports is reconnaissance to map open services, the hallmark of a port scan. It is not proof of a breach by itself, nor normal backup or DNS transfer behavior.

q: A critical database server needs detection of unauthorized file changes and local privilege escalation attempts. Which solution BEST fits this requirement?
options: A host-based IDS on the database server
A network IDS on the perimeter only
explain: A host-based IDS sees local events such as file integrity changes and privilege escalation that perimeter network sensors miss. Perimeter tools lack that host-level visibility into local activity.

q: Fake credentials and database records planted to alert the team when they are touched are an example of which technique?
explain: Honey tokens are decoy data items that generate alerts when accessed, revealing intruders who have passed other controls. The other options are access, isolation, and tunneling mechanisms, not decoys.

q: A contractor laptop connects to the network but its antivirus is outdated and patches are missing. Under posture-based NAC, what should happen?
options: Disable the contractor account in the directory only
Permanently ban the device from all networks
Grant full access and log nothing
Place it in a quarantine network until it is remediated
explain: Posture checks route noncompliant devices to a limited remediation network until they meet health policy. Full access ignores the risk, and a permanent ban is disproportionate to a fixable state.

q: Which TWO design choices BEST protect a public-facing application that must read data from an internal database? (Choose two.)
options: Permit only the application tier inward and deny all other DMZ-to-internal traffic
Place the database itself in the DMZ
Allow any DMZ host to reach any internal port
Place the application in a DMZ and allow only its specific database port inward
explain: Tiered placement plus narrowly scoped rules let the application reach only the database service it needs. Putting the database in the DMZ or allowing broad inward access exposes far more than required.

q: Where is a VPN concentrator MOST appropriately placed in a typical perimeter design?
options: On the desk of each user as a hardware token
At the network edge where remote tunnels terminate before traffic enters trusted zones
Behind the internal core with no firewall in front of it
explain: The concentrator terminates tunnels at the edge so decrypted traffic can be inspected and filtered before entering trusted networks. It is gateway infrastructure, not a token or storage component.

q: A company already has an NGFW, but attackers keep exploiting input validation flaws in its web application that the NGFW passes as legitimate HTTPS. What is the BEST next step?
options: Block all HTTPS traffic at the perimeter
Remove the NGFW and rely on patching alone
Add a WAF tuned to the application in front of the web tier
Move the web servers onto the internal LAN
explain: A WAF inspects application-layer inputs that an NGFW treats as valid web traffic, addressing the specific gap. Removing layered controls, exposing servers on the LAN, or blocking HTTPS harms security or the business.

q: A team wants visibility into attacks that have already passed the perimeter firewall and are moving toward internal servers. Where should an additional network IDS sensor be placed?
options: Inside the firewall on the internal side of the perimeter
On the public web server in the DMZ only
Only outside the firewall facing the Internet
Disconnected in a lab for testing
explain: An inside sensor sees traffic that survived perimeter filtering and reveals what is actually reaching internal systems. An outside-only sensor drowns in Internet noise and cannot show what got through.

q: A research team wants detailed attacker tooling and techniques and accepts higher risk and maintenance effort. Which decoy BEST matches this goal?
options: A DNS sinkhole for malware domains
A low-interaction honeypot that emulates a few ports
A high-interaction honeypot running a real operating system
A honey token in a database table
explain: A high-interaction honeypot runs real services so researchers can observe full attacker behavior, at greater risk and cost; grouped honeypots form a honeynet. Low-interaction emulations yield far less detail.

q: A legacy design routes all external access through one host with two network interfaces and disabled IP forwarding, forcing connections through proxy software. What is this host?
options: A load balancer in active-active mode
explain: A dual-homed host straddles two networks with forwarding disabled so traffic must pass through its proxy services. It is not air-gapped: an air gap means no network connection at all between systems.

q: Attack traffic consists of valid-looking HTTP requests at rates each connection could plausibly generate, exhausting application resources. Which defense is MOST appropriate?
options: Blocking all ICMP at the router
Application-layer rate limiting with a WAF and caching
explain: Application-layer floods mimic legitimate requests, so WAF rate controls, caching, and request validation are needed. Network-layer UDP or ICMP filters and DHCP changes do not address HTTP request exhaustion.

q: A global service suffers repeated volumetric DDoS attacks that saturate a single data center link. Which architecture change MOST improves resilience?
options: Advertise the service by anycast across multiple sites with scrubbing capacity
Host the service on one larger server
Move the service behind a home broadband connection
explain: Anycast spreads attack traffic across many sites so no single link absorbs the full volume, and scrubbing filters malicious traffic. Concentrating the service in one place makes saturation easier.

q: Users on a conference network are presented with invalid certificates when visiting banking sites, suggesting an on-path attack. What is the BEST immediate guidance?
options: Do not proceed, disconnect, and use a trusted connection or VPN
Share credentials quickly before the session expires
Disable certificate validation in the browser permanently
Accept the certificates to maintain productivity
explain: Invalid certificates during suspected interception mean the connection cannot be trusted; leaving the network or tunneling over a trusted path protects credentials. Accepting or disabling validation completes the attack.

q: Before deploying access points in a new warehouse, a team maps signal strength, interference sources, and dead zones. What is this process called?
explain: A site survey measures coverage, interference, and capacity needs so access points are placed correctly. It is a design activity, distinct from penetration testing or hunting for rogue devices, though it can reveal them.

q: An attacker sets up a laptop as an access point with the corporate SSID near a branch office, and employee devices connect automatically. Which control combination MOST reduces this evil twin risk?
options: Mutual EAP-TLS authentication and wireless IDS monitoring
explain: Mutual certificate authentication prevents clients from trusting an impostor server, and wireless IDS detects the rogue radio. SSID hiding, MAC filtering, WEP, and portals offer no real authentication of the network.

q: A hospital must assess unmanaged medical devices that cannot run endpoint software before granting network access. Which NAC approach BEST fits?
options: Agentless assessment using network behavior and fingerprinting
Requiring each device to join the domain
explain: Agentless NAC evaluates devices through scanning, fingerprinting, and traffic behavior when software cannot be installed. Agent-only and domain-join approaches exclude exactly the devices that must be managed.

q: A bank requires a password plus a hardware token to access the wire-transfer system. An auditor asks whether this is multifactor authentication. It is, because:
options: Passwords plus tokens equal three factors
It combines two different factor types: something you know and something you have
Two passwords are always stronger than one
explain: MFA requires two or more *different* factor categories. Password (know) + hardware token (have) qualifies. Two passwords would be single-factor done twice; tokens are phishing-resistant but not unphishable; this is two factors, not three.

q: A hospital system grants access based on role (doctor, nurse), department, shift time, and whether the patient is assigned to that clinician. Which access control model is this?
explain: ABAC evaluates multiple attributes of the subject, object, and environment against policy. Pure RBAC would stop at the role; the shift-time and patient-assignment attributes make this attribute-based.

q: Engineers authenticate once to the corporate identity provider and are then signed into the cloud console, the ticketing system, and the code repository without re-authenticating. The ticketing system is run by a separate company that trusts the corporate IdP. Which two concepts are in play?
explain: One authentication reused across systems is SSO; the cross-organization trust between the corporate IdP and the vendor's service is federation (typically via SAML). Kerberos/TACACS+ don't span orgs this way.

q: After a reorganization, dozens of transferred employees retain access to their former departments' file shares. What is this failure called, and what control prevents recurrence?
explain: Accumulated unneeded access after role changes is privilege creep. The preventive control is the joiner-mover-leaver process with periodic access reviews/recertification so managers confirm continued need.

q: A Kerberos deployment fails every morning until clocks are resynchronized. What is the root cause?
options: Kerberos requires synchronized time (5-minute skew tolerance)
The KDC does not support AES
Ticket expiration is set too short
explain: Kerberos timestamps tickets to prevent replay, so clients and the KDC must agree on time within about 5 minutes. Clock drift breaks authentication — the single most-tested Kerberos operational fact.

Identification comes first: the user claims an identity, usually with a username. Authentication then proves that claim, authorization applies permissions, and accountability records actions. Authentication cannot verify a claim that has not yet been made.
options: Accountability, because logging starts before access begins
Authentication, because credentials are verified before any claim is made
Identification, because the user first claims an identity such as a username
Authorization, because permissions are checked before identity is claimed
q: In the IAAA model, which step occurs first when a user accesses a system?

explain: Entering a username is identification, the claim of identity. No proof has been presented yet, so authentication has not occurred, and authorization and accountability follow successful authentication.
q: A help desk analyst enters a username at a login prompt but has not yet typed a password. Which IAAA process has occurred so far?

explain: Authorization determines what a verified identity is permitted to do, such as opening a folder. Authentication only proved who the user is; it does not by itself grant any rights or permissions.
q: After verifying a user's password, a system checks whether that user may open the payroll folder. Which IAAA process is this?

explain: Accountability depends on auditing: logs that reliably associate actions with the authenticated identity who performed them. ACLs support authorization, while complexity and lockout support authentication strength.
options: Audit logging that ties actions to an identity
q: Which mechanism primarily supports accountability in the IAAA model?

explain: Accountability means actions can be traced to the identity that performed them, which requires tamper-resistant audit logs. Password rules strengthen authentication, and accountability follows identification, authentication, and authorization.
options: It is achieved mainly by making passwords longer and more complex
It requires that actions be traceable to a specific authenticated identity
It occurs before identification in the access sequence
It depends on audit logs being protected from tampering by those they monitor
q: Which two statements correctly describe accountability in IAAA? (Choose two.)

explain: Authentication proves who the user is; authorization separately decides what that user may access, guided by least privilege. Treating the two as one step would grant far more access than the job requires.
options: Authorization is only needed for administrators, not regular users
Successful authentication disables the need for auditing
Authentication should occur after authorization in the IAAA sequence
Authentication and authorization are separate; proof of identity grants no rights by itself
q: A manager insists that because an employee authenticated successfully, the employee should automatically be able to read every file. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

explain: Shared accounts destroy accountability: logs show the shared identity acted, not which person used it. Authentication still functions and permissions still work, but individual responsibility can no longer be established.
options: Identification, because no username is presented
Accountability, because actions cannot be tied to one person
Authorization, because permissions cannot be assigned
Authentication, because passwords no longer work
q: An organization finds that shared administrator accounts make incident investigations inconclusive. Which IAAA element is most directly undermined?

explain: The sequence is identification (claim), authentication (proof), authorization (permission check), and accountability (logging of actions). Any order placing authorization before authentication would grant rights to an unproven identity.
q: What is the correct order of the IAAA processes during a typical logon and file access?

explain: A fingerprint is inherence (something you are, Type 3) and a PIN is knowledge (something you know, Type 1). Combining different factor types is true multifactor authentication, unlike two factors of the same type.
options: Inherence and knowledge, which is true multifactor authentication
q: A user unlocks a phone with a fingerprint and then enters a PIN. Which factor types are combined?

explain: Both items are knowledge factors (Type 1), so only one factor type is present. True multifactor authentication combines different types, such as knowledge plus possession or inherence. Two steps using the same type add limited strength.
options: Both factors are the same type: something you know
Multifactor authentication requires at least three factors
Passwords cannot be used in multifactor schemes
Email is too slow to count as a factor
q: A login requires a password and then a second password sent by email. Why does this NOT qualify as true multifactor authentication?
