explain: RAID 1 is mirroring, writing identical data to two disks for redundancy. RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy, while RAID 5 and 6 distribute parity across disks instead of keeping full copies.
q: Two disks contain identical copies of the same data so work continues if one disk fails. Which RAID level is this?

explain: RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity and tolerates one disk failure. RAID 0 has no fault tolerance, RAID 1 mirrors pairs, and RAID 10 combines mirroring with striping across multiple pairs.
q: An array stripes data across three disks with distributed parity and survives any single disk failure. Which RAID level is this?

explain: RAID 0 stripes data across disks for performance with no redundancy, so any single disk failure destroys the volume. RAID 1, 5, and 6 all provide redundancy that survives at least one disk failure.
q: A video editing workstation uses an array that stripes data for speed, but one disk failure loses the entire volume. Which RAID level is in use?

explain: RAID 6 uses dual distributed parity and tolerates two concurrent disk failures. RAID 5 tolerates only one failure, RAID 1 mirrors a single pair, and RAID 0 tolerates none.
q: A storage administrator needs an array that can survive two simultaneous disk failures using dual parity. What should be selected?

explain: Redundancy removes single points of failure and load balancing spreads work across active servers so one loss does not stop service. A lone server is itself a single point of failure, and disabling monitoring hides failures.
options: Redundant components that remove single points of failure
A single high-capacity server with no spare parts
Load balancing across multiple active servers
q: Which measures improve a critical service ability to keep operating despite component failures? (Choose two.)

explain: MTBF, mean time between failures, measures average operating time before failure and indicates reliability. MTTR measures repair time, while RPO and RTO are recovery objectives for data loss and downtime.
q: A vendor states a drive model averages 50,000 hours of operation before a failure occurs. Which metric is this?

explain: MTTR, mean time to repair, is the average time to restore a failed system to operation. MTBF measures time between failures, not repair duration, and detection time covers only discovery, not full restoration.
q: After each hardware failure, a support team averages four hours to diagnose, repair, and return the system to service. Which metric is this?

explain: Fault tolerance means the system continues operating without interruption despite component failure through redundancy. High availability minimizes downtime but can still involve brief outages, unlike true fault tolerance.
q: A service must keep running without interruption even when a component fails, using duplicate components that take over instantly, rather than merely restoring service quickly after an outage. What design goal is this?

explain: Load balancing distributes requests across all available servers, using idle capacity and improving resilience. More disk does not relieve compute load, restarts cause outages, and blocking users denies legitimate service.
options: Blocking half of the incoming users
Load balancing across all application servers
Adding more disk space to the busy server
q: Web traffic spikes overwhelm one application server while two identical servers sit underused. What operational control BEST resolves this?

explain: One component whose failure disables everything dependent on it is a single point of failure requiring redundancy. Calling it defense in depth is the opposite of reality, and it is not acceptable without explicit risk treatment.
options: An acceptable documented risk by default
q: An availability review finds that every critical application depends on one authentication server with no replica. How is this BEST characterized?

explain: Capacity management monitors utilization trends and plans expansion before resources exhaust and performance fails. Incident response reacts to events, freezes halt changes, and media destruction is unrelated to growth planning.
options: Capacity and resource management with trending and planned expansion
q: Month after month, a file server runs near full disk and response times degrade during peak reporting. What operations discipline addresses this trend?

explain: Disabling unnecessary services reduces attack surface, a core hardening practice. Leaving an unneeded vulnerable service running, even with a password or new subnet, retains risk the business does not need.
options: Give it a stronger password only
Move it to a different subnet
Disable or remove the unnecessary service
Leave it running for possible future use
q: A hardening review finds a production server running an unused file-sharing service with known vulnerabilities. What is the BEST operational action?

explain: Deploying vetted gold images and disabling unused ports and services both reduce attack surface consistently. Enabling defaults expands exposure, and shared admin accounts destroy accountability.
options: Applying a vetted secure gold image to new systems
Enabling every default service for convenience
Sharing one administrator account among the team
q: Which practices are part of sound system hardening operations? (Choose two.)

explain: Dual control requires two people to perform an action together so no individual can complete it alone. Split knowledge divides information such as a password, while rotation and vacations address fraud detection over time.
q: Launching a nuclear facility system requires two authorized operators to turn keys simultaneously so neither can act alone. What control is this?

explain: Split knowledge divides a secret or credential so no single person holds the whole. Dual control requires simultaneous action by two people, which differs from each holding only part of the needed information.
q: A safe combination is divided so one officer knows the first half and another knows the second half; both halves are required to open it. What control is this?

explain: Job rotation exposes irregularities when a new person reviews inherited work and builds cross-training. It does not replace logging or separation of duties, and it reduces but cannot guarantee against collusion.
options: It removes the need for separation of duties
It helps detect fraud and errors and cross-trains staff
It eliminates the need for logging
It guarantees no collusion can occur
q: Operations rotates administrators among systems every quarter, and the practice surfaces an irregular change pattern left by a previous administrator. What is a PRIMARY benefit of job rotation?

explain: Time-limited, individually attributable vendor access with MFA and logging, disabled afterward, limits exposure. Permanent shared accounts and shared passwords remove accountability and leave standing attack paths.
options: Share an employee password with the vendor
Leave vendor access enabled year-round for convenience
Enable a named, time-limited account with approval, MFA, and session logging, then disable it after the work
Give the vendor a shared permanent administrator account
q: A vendor needs remote access for maintenance next week. What is the BEST operational handling of that access?

explain: Visitor logging, identity verification, badging, and escorting in secure areas maintain physical accountability. Unescorted access, after-hours solo entry, or shared door codes defeat physical access control.
options: Ask the visitor to return after hours alone
Sign the visitor in, verify identity, issue a visitor badge, and provide an escort in secure areas
Let the visitor enter unescorted with a master badge
Give the visitor the door code for future visits
q: A visitor arrives to repair a printer in a secure area. What should operations require?

explain: Secure media handling requires sensitive media to be stored in locked, controlled locations, and clean desk practice forbids leaving it exposed. Patching, load balancing, and change control govern different operations.
options: Clean desk and secure media handling
q: An auditor finds backup tapes with customer data left on an open desk overnight. Which operational practice was violated?

explain: Blocking mode prevented the unauthorized egress while logging created evidence for triage and trend analysis. It did not encrypt data at rest, terminate the account automatically, or back up the blocked file.
options: Encryption of data at rest and faster uploads
Automatic termination of the employee account
Backup of the file to the cloud drive
Prevention of the exfiltration and an auditable record for review
q: A DLP system in blocking mode stops an employee from uploading a file containing customer records to a personal cloud drive, and logs the attempt. What two functions did operations gain?

explain: Alert fatigue occurs when excessive false or low-value alerts desensitize analysts so genuine alerts are missed. The remedy is tuning and prioritization, not retention changes, encryption, or backup fixes.
options: Alert fatigue caused by poor tuning
q: A SOC analyst receives hundreds of identical low-value alerts each shift and begins ignoring the queue, missing a real alert buried among them. What operational problem is this?

explain: Gold images deploy a vetted, consistent, hardened configuration every time, eliminating build drift. Personal preferences recreate inconsistency, and rebuilding after incidents is reactive rather than preventive.
options: Let each administrator document personal preferences
Deploy from an approved gold image with a secure baseline configuration
q: New servers are built manually and each ends up with different settings, causing repeated incidents. What operational practice BEST standardizes builds?

explain: Verification confirms the patch applied correctly, removed the vulnerability, preserved functionality, and is documented. Evaluation happens before selection, and development and decommissioning are not patch lifecycle confirmation steps.
q: After deploying a patch, operations confirms the vulnerability is gone, the application still functions, and the patch level is recorded. Which patch lifecycle phase is this?

explain: Immutable and air-gapped offline copies survive ransomware that spreads through the network and alters reachable data. A mounted sole copy and real-time replicated shares are encrypted along with production.
options: Store an air-gapped offline copy of critical backups
Maintain immutable backup copies that cannot be altered
Rely solely on file shares replicated in real time
Keep the only backup copy mounted on the production network
q: Which backup protections MOST help an organization recover after ransomware encrypts production systems? (Choose two.)

explain: Signature-based detection depends on current vendor signature updates to recognize new attacks. Defragmentation, password rotation, and tape rotation do not supply detection content for emerging threats.
q: An IDS begins missing a newly published attack pattern because its detection content has not been refreshed in months. What maintenance was neglected?

explain: Continuous monitoring provides ongoing awareness of controls, vulnerabilities, and changes so drift is caught quickly. Annual or point-in-time reviews leave long blind periods between assessments.
q: Instead of reviewing security posture once a year, an organization continuously collects and assesses control and vulnerability data to detect drift promptly. What is this practice?
A code review finds user input concatenated directly into SQL queries across a legacy application. What is the vulnerability, and what is the BEST remediation?
options: Broken access control; add role checks
SQL injection; rewrite queries with parameterized statements and validate input
explain: String-concatenated SQL is textbook SQL injection. The definitive fix is parameterized queries/prepared statements (plus allowlist input validation) — not blacklisting, not encoding (that's for XSS), and not decommissioning a fixable app. ---
Waterfall is sequential with phase gates, making late changes expensive. Agile is iterative, spiral is risk-driven and iterative, and prototyping builds early mockups for feedback.
q: A project uses a sequential lifecycle where each phase must be completed and approved before the next begins, and late changes are costly. Which model is in use?

explain: Agile with scrum uses short iterative sprints, daily stand-ups, and a reprioritized backlog. Waterfall is sequential, spiral centers on risk analysis cycles, and the V-model pairs phases with testing.
q: A team delivers working software in two-week sprints, holds daily stand-ups, and reprioritizes a backlog each iteration. Which lifecycle model BEST describes this approach?

explain: Defining security requirements in the requirements phase is cheapest and most effective because design and code build on them. Adding them in testing or later requires expensive rework.
q: During which SDLC phase should security requirements be defined to be MOST cost-effective?

explain: Security must be integrated across the entire lifecycle starting at requirements; late testing finds flaws when fixes cost the most. Production controls and operations ownership do not replace secure development.
options: Testing alone satisfies secure development requirements
Defer security to the operations team after go-live
Agree, since production controls will compensate
Security activities belong throughout the lifecycle, starting with requirements
q: A development manager proposes adding security testing only just before production release to save time. What is the BEST response from a security professional?

explain: The spiral model is risk-driven, with risk analysis in each loop determining continuation. Waterfall has no iterative risk loops, prototyping focuses on user feedback, and scrum focuses on backlog delivery.
q: An organization wants a lifecycle model that explicitly evaluates risk at each iteration before deciding whether to proceed. Which model BEST fits?

explain: Prototyping builds an early working model to validate requirements and workflows with users. Waterfall forbids this overlap, DevSecOps is a culture and pipeline practice, and spiral centers on risk analysis.
q: A team builds a quick throwaway user interface so stakeholders can validate workflows before full development begins. This is an example of which approach?

explain: Threat modeling in design identifies assets, threats, and mitigations while changes are still cheap. It does not replace later testing and is not primarily about language selection or training.
options: To identify threats and design mitigations before code is written
To replace penetration testing after release
q: What is the PRIMARY goal of threat modeling during the design phase?

explain: DevSecOps integrates security into DevOps pipelines with automated checks and shared responsibility, shifting security left. Waterfall is sequential, while polyinstantiation and escrow are unrelated database and assurance concepts.
q: An organization embeds security scans into its CI/CD pipeline, treats security checks as code, and makes security a shared responsibility of developers and operations. This BEST describes which concept?

explain: Shift left means moving security activities such as threat modeling and code review earlier, where defects are cheaper to fix. It does not refer to facilities, traffic, or transferring ownership to operations.
options: Performing security activities earlier in the lifecycle
Moving testing to the operations team
Shifting production traffic to a backup site
Moving the data center to a new location
q: What does the term shift left mean in secure development?

explain: Flaws found in design are cheapest to fix before code exists. Waiting until deployment, an incident, or an upgrade multiplies cost and exposure, which is the core shift-left principle.
options: Now, during design, before code is written
q: A secure design review finds that a proposed architecture stores credentials in plaintext. When is this flaw CHEAPEST to remediate?

explain: In agile, the product owner prioritizes the backlog with input from the whole team, so security stories compete visibly for priority. Auditors, the scrum master alone, or the customer alone do not own backlog content.
options: The product owner working with the whole team, including security input
q: In an agile team, who is PRIMARILY responsible for ensuring security user stories are included in the sprint backlog?

explain: A secure design review evaluates architecture against security requirements before coding, catching structural flaws early. Later tests validate implementation but cannot as cheaply fix design errors.
q: A firm requires a formal sign-off of security architecture before coding begins on a high-risk payment system. Which activity BEST provides this assurance?

explain: Parameterized queries separate code from data so input can never alter query logic, fixing the root cause. A WAF is only defense-in-depth, and renaming tables or hiding errors does not stop injection.
q: Which of the following is the MOST effective control against SQL injection?

explain: Reflected XSS occurs when input is immediately returned and executed without proper output encoding. Stored XSS persists the payload, SQL injection targets databases, and SSRF forces server requests.
q: A web application reflects user input back into a page without encoding, allowing script execution in victims browsers. Which vulnerability is present?

explain: Stored XSS persists the payload on the server so it executes for all viewers. Reflected and DOM-based variants are not stored server-side, and CSRF tricks a browser into making unwanted requests.
q: An attacker stores a malicious script in a comment field that executes for every user who views the page. This is BEST classified as which attack?

explain: Broken access control ranks first in the current OWASP Top 10, reflecting how common authorization failures are. Injection, misconfiguration, and cryptographic failures rank lower.
q: According to recent OWASP Top 10 awareness, which category ranks FIRST?

explain: Accessing another users object without an authorization check is broken access control, specifically insecure direct object reference. No injection, crypto failure, or component flaw is involved.
q: A user changes an account ID in a URL from 1001 to 1002 and views another customers data without any authorization check. Which OWASP category does this BEST represent?

explain: An allowlist that permits only the expected format, five digits, rejects everything else and is strongest. Denylists miss novel attacks, client-side checks are bypassable, and a firewall is not a substitute.
options: Allowlist permitting only five numeric digits
No validation if a firewall is present
q: Which input validation approach is MOST secure for a field that should contain only a five-digit postal code?

explain: Server-side validation is authoritative because attackers control the client and can bypass browser checks entirely. Client-side validation improves usability only and never replaces server enforcement.
options: Yes, server-side validation is authoritative because client controls can be bypassed
Only if the application uses cookies
q: A developer implements validation in the browser for usability and asks whether server-side validation is still needed. What is the CORRECT answer?

explain: SSRF occurs when an attacker makes the server issue requests to unintended internal destinations. XSS executes script in browsers, buffer overflows corrupt memory, and session fixation sets a known session ID.
q: An application accepts a URL parameter and the server fetches an internal metadata endpoint, exposing cloud credentials. Which vulnerability is this?

explain: Output encoding converts special characters so browsers treat data as text, not code, preventing XSS. Compression, encryption at rest, and indexing are unrelated purposes.
options: To prevent user data from being interpreted as executable code
q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of output encoding?

explain: Canonicalization attacks exploit inconsistent normalization, where different components interpret encoded input differently. Race conditions involve timing, session fixation involves session IDs, and inference targets databases.
q: An attacker submits input using double URL encoding so a filter sees a harmless string but the application decodes it into a path traversal. Which attack technique is used?

explain: Verbose errors leak internal details attackers use to plan injection and other attacks, so errors should be generic to users and detailed only in protected logs. Performance and cost are secondary.
q: A production error page displays a full stack trace, database connection string, and server version to end users. What is the PRIMARY security concern?

explain: HttpOnly prevents script access to the cookie and Secure restricts it to HTTPS, together reducing theft. A wildcard domain broadens exposure and long expiration increases the window for misuse.
q: Which cookie attributes BEST protect a session cookie from theft via script and from transmission over plaintext connections? (Choose two.)

explain: Session fixation forces a known session ID on the victim before authentication, then reuses it; the defense is issuing a new ID after login. Sniffing steals an existing ID rather than planting one.
q: An attacker sets a session ID, tricks a victim into logging in with it, and then reuses the known ID. Which attack is this?

explain: Unchecked copying into a fixed buffer is a classic buffer overflow, a memory safety flaw. Injection, access control, and misconfiguration do not involve memory corruption.
q: A program written in C copies user input into a fixed-size buffer without length checking, allowing memory corruption. Which vulnerability class is MOST directly involved?

explain: TOCTOU exploits the window between checking a condition and using the resource, here swapping the file after the check. The other flaws involve memory, encoding, or sessions, not timing.
q: An attacker checks whether a file exists and then opens it, but swaps the file for a symbolic link in between the two operations. Which flaw is exploited?

explain: Least privilege requires only the rights needed for the job; excess database rights amplify any compromise. Defense in depth and fail secure are not about account rights sizing.
q: An application service account is granted full database administrator rights although it only needs to read and write two tables. Which principle is violated?

explain: Using a component with a known critical flaw is the vulnerable and outdated components category. The issue is the unpatched dependency itself, not access control, injection, or logging design.
q: A retailer discovers its application uses a logging library with a known critical remote code execution flaw. Which OWASP category BEST covers this risk?

explain: Default credentials and unnecessary sample apps are classic security misconfiguration. No crypto weakness, server-side request, or integrity verification failure is described.
q: A newly deployed web server still has its default administrator password and sample applications enabled. Which OWASP category is MOST relevant?

explain: Weak hashing and plaintext transport of sensitive data are cryptographic failures. Access control and injection concern authorization and query handling, not protection of data in storage and transit.
q: An application stores passwords using a fast unsalted hash and transmits them over HTTP on an internal page. Which OWASP category BEST applies?

explain: Fixing code with parameterized queries and validation removes the flaw itself; WAF rules are defense-in-depth that can be bypassed. Geo-blocking and extra logging do not remediate the vulnerability.
options: Fixing the code with parameterized queries and validation
Blocking the affected country at the firewall
q: A security engineer must choose between fixing injection flaws in code or adding more WAF rules to block attack patterns. Which approach addresses the ROOT cause?

explain: SAST statically analyzes source or bytecode without running the application, finding flaws early. DAST tests a running app, IAST instruments a running app, and RASP protects at runtime.
q: Which testing technique analyzes source code for vulnerabilities WITHOUT executing the application?

explain: DAST exercises the running application externally without source access, finding runtime and configuration flaws. SAST needs code, signing verifies origin, and SCA inventories components.
q: A tester attacks a running web application from the outside with no access to source code, simulating a real attacker. Which technique is this?

explain: IAST places agents inside the running application to observe execution during testing, combining static and dynamic insight. SAST and DAST lack internal instrumentation, and a WAF filters traffic.
q: Which technology instruments the running application from inside to report vulnerabilities while tests execute?

explain: RASP runs inside the application in production and can block exploits as they occur. SAST is pre-release analysis, an SBOM is an inventory document, and repo scanners check stored code.
q: Which technology is embedded in the application runtime and can BLOCK an attack in real time in production?

explain: Code signing provides authenticity and integrity, proving who published the software and that it is unmodified. It does not encrypt code, speed execution, or replace scanning.
options: To verify the softwares origin and that it has not been altered
q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of code signing for software releases?

explain: Sandboxing confines code to a restricted environment, limiting harm and enabling observation. Signing verifies origin, polyinstantiation is a database concept, and escrow holds source with a third party.
q: Untrusted code from the internet is executed inside an isolated environment with restricted system access so its behavior can be observed safely. This control is known as which of the following?

explain: An SBOM lists all components and versions so teams can locate affected software rapidly. Threat models and data flow diagrams show design, not a component inventory.
q: A team needs an inventory of every third-party component and library in its product to respond quickly when a new vulnerability is announced. Which artifact BEST provides this?

explain: SCA scans dependencies against vulnerability databases and license data. Dynamic analysis tests runtime behavior, load testing measures performance, and threat modeling analyzes design.
q: Which tool or process identifies known vulnerabilities in open-source libraries an application depends on?

explain: Production data must never enter lower environments without sanitization or masking because test systems have weaker controls. Using raw data, committing it, or adding internet access all increase exposure.
options: The data must be sanitized or masked so real personal data is not exposed in test
The data must be published to the code repository
The test environment must be given internet access
q: A developer copies live customer records into the test environment to reproduce a bug. What MUST happen FIRST under secure environment rules?

explain: Proper separation promotes code from development to test to production through controlled change processes. Shared or production-first arrangements destroy isolation and change control.
options: A single shared environment for all stages
Development, test, production with controlled promotion between them
q: Which set of environments, in order, BEST reflects proper separation before production release?

explain: Hardening build servers and signing artifacts with verification protect pipeline integrity end to end. Broad production access and disabling logging weaken security and accountability.
options: Harden and restrict access to build servers
Sign build artifacts and verify signatures before deployment
Give all developers production database access
q: An attacker compromises a build server and inserts malicious code into artifacts that are later deployed as trusted. Which defenses MOST directly address this pipeline risk? (Choose two.)

explain: A committed secret must be treated as compromised: revoke and rotate it, remove it from history, and use a secrets manager going forward. Private repos, renames, and comments do not undo exposure.
options: Revoke and rotate the key, purge it from history, and move secrets to a managed secrets store
Add a comment warning others not to use the key
Leave the key since the repo is private
q: A pipeline configuration file contains a plaintext cloud access key that was committed to the repository. What is the BEST immediate and long-term response?

explain: Branch protection and required reviews enforce change control and create an audit trail for code changes. Version control speeds no compilation and cannot automatically eliminate bugs.
options: Controlled, auditable changes with peer review before merging
q: What is the PRIMARY security benefit of using a version control system with branch protection and required reviews for application code?

explain: Change control requires testing, approval, and documentation for code changes, even urgent ones via an expedited path. The bypass is procedural, not a coding or signing failure.
q: A critical hotfix is pushed directly to production code without testing, approval, or documentation. Which control has been bypassed?

explain: Views act as access control by exposing only authorized columns and rows to each role. Replication copies data, disabling logs removes accountability, and polyinstantiation handles multilevel records.
options: A view limited to permitted columns and rows
q: A database administrator restricts clerks to seeing only customer names and order totals, hiding salary and national ID columns. Which database mechanism BEST implements this?

explain: Aggregation creates sensitive insight by combining many individually innocuous items. Inference deduces from queries and responses, polyinstantiation stores multiple versions, and pharming redirects web traffic.
q: An analyst combines publicly available headcount data, office closure notices, and shift schedules to deduce which plant will be shut down, information classified as sensitive. Which attack concept does this illustrate?

explain: An inference attack deduces protected values from legitimate query results and system responses. Aggregation combines separate data sets, while overflow and fixation are application flaws.
q: A user repeatedly queries a statistics database with carefully chosen criteria until the responses reveal a single employees salary, even though direct salary queries are blocked. Which attack is this?

explain: Polyinstantiation maintains multiple instances of a record at different security levels to prevent inference and signaling. Aggregation, mining, and normalization address analysis or structure, not cover records.
q: In a multilevel secure database, two records with the same primary key exist at different classification levels so lower-cleared users see a cover story. This technique is called which of the following?

explain: Warehouses concentrate large volumes of historical data, increasing aggregation, inference, and breach impact risks. The concern is data concentration, not coding or session flaws.
options: Data warehousing concentration and mining exposure
q: A company consolidates years of sales data into a warehouse for trend analysis, inadvertently creating a single high-value target containing sensitive patterns. Which risk is MOST increased?

explain: OLTP systems handle many concurrent short transactions on current data, such as order entry. OLAP and warehouses support complex analytical queries over historical data.
q: Which system is optimized for high-volume day-to-day transaction processing with current records?

explain: Encryption at rest plus least-privilege access control together protect stored data. Direct broad access defeats authorization, and storing keys beside the data defeats encryption.
options: Storing the encryption key in the same table as the data
Granting all application users direct table access
Strict access control based on least privilege
Encryption of sensitive data at rest
q: Which controls BEST protect sensitive data stored in an application database at the concept level? (Choose two.)

explain: Worms self-propagate across networks without a host file or user action. Viruses need a host, trojans need user deception, and logic bombs wait for a trigger condition.
q: Malicious code spreads across a network by itself without needing a host file or user action. Which type is this?

explain: Macro viruses embed in documents and spreadsheets and spread when files are opened and shared. Worms self-propagate on networks, rootkits hide presence, and ransomware encrypts for payment.
q: A user opens a spreadsheet and embedded code infects other documents on the system. Which malware type is MOST likely?

explain: Polymorphic malware mutates its appearance each infection to defeat signature matching. Multipartite uses multiple infection methods, macro viruses live in documents, and trojans disguise themselves as useful software.
q: Malware changes its code signature with each infection while keeping the same payload, evading signature-based detection. Which type is this?

explain: Multipartite malware uses multiple infection vectors, such as boot sector plus files, complicating eradication. Polymorphic refers to code mutation, and macro viruses infect documents.
q: A virus infects both the boot sector and executable files, making full removal difficult. Which type is this?

explain: A trojan appears useful or entertaining while hiding a malicious payload. Worms self-propagate, logic bombs trigger on conditions, and polymorphic describes mutation, not deception.
q: A free game download secretly installs a remote access tool that lets an attacker control the machine. The game itself is BEST described as which of the following?

explain: A logic bomb stays dormant until a specific condition or trigger occurs, here removal from the employee file. Worms spread actively, macro viruses infect documents, and backdoors provide ongoing access.
q: A disgruntled developer plants code that deletes payroll data if his name is ever removed from the employee file. This is an example of which threat?

explain: A backdoor is a hidden method of bypassing normal authentication, such as an undocumented account. Logic bombs trigger on conditions, worms self-propagate, and rootkits hide malicious presence.
q: A vendor leaves an undocumented maintenance account with a hardcoded password in a delivered application. This is BEST classified as which of the following?

explain: Rootkits conceal malicious activity, often at kernel level, undermining trust in the system itself. Trojans rely on deception, macro viruses on documents, and logic bombs on triggers.
q: Malware operating at the kernel level hides its processes and files from the operating system and security tools. Which type is this?

explain: Ransomware encrypts data and extorts payment, often targeting backups to force payment. Keylogging steals input, macro infection spreads via documents, and propagation alone does not encrypt for ransom.
q: Systems across a hospital suddenly display a demand for payment after files are encrypted and backups are targeted. Which malware behavior is occurring?

explain: Signature detection matches known patterns, so novel malware has no signature until vendors publish one. Heuristic and behavioral methods help fill this gap but can produce false positives.
options: No signature exists yet for the unknown sample
q: Why does signature-based antivirus FAIL against brand-new malware?

explain: Heuristic analysis judges likely maliciousness from behavior or traits, which catches new threats but can false-positive on legitimate software. Signature matching would not flag an unknown clean file this way.
q: An antivirus flags a clean new internal tool as malicious because its behavior resembles malware. Which detection method and drawback are illustrated?

explain: Application allowlisting permits only approved executables and blocks all else by default, strongly limiting malware. Denylisting and signature tools only block what is already known to be bad.
q: On high-security workstations, only approved, signed applications may execute and everything else is blocked by default. Which malware control is this?

explain: CMM Level 1 Initial describes ad hoc, hero-dependent processes. Higher levels add repeatability, organization-wide definition, measurement, and continuous optimization.
q: In the Capability Maturity Model, an organization whose processes are ad hoc, chaotic, and dependent on individuals is at which level?

explain: Level 4 Managed applies quantitative measurement and statistical control to processes. Level 2 is project-level repeatability and Level 3 is organization-wide defined processes without quantitative control.
q: An organization measures its development processes quantitatively and uses the data to control process performance. Which CMMI level BEST matches?

explain: OWASP SAMM provides a maturity model for software assurance with defined practices and levels. ITIL covers service management and COBIT covers governance, not software security maturity specifically.
q: A software team wants a framework of security activities and maturity levels specifically for building security into development, with practices organized by maturity. Which framework BEST fits?

explain: BSIMM is observational, describing activities actually practiced by participating firms. SAMM is prescriptive, while waterfall and spiral are lifecycle models, not maturity studies.
q: A manager studies what peer organizations actually do for software security by reviewing an observational study of real-world security initiatives. Which model is she MOST likely using?

explain: Acceptance testing validates the delivered system against agreed criteria, including security requirements, before acceptance. Threat modeling is a design activity and escrow concerns source availability.
q: Before final acceptance of a delivered system, the customer verifies that all documented security requirements and acceptance criteria have been met. This activity is BEST described as which of the following?

explain: Software escrow deposits source code with a third party for release under defined conditions such as vendor failure. Signing proves origin, copyleft governs distribution terms, and sandboxing isolates execution.
q: A buyer requires a critical vendors source code to be held by a neutral third party, releasable if the vendor goes out of business. This arrangement is known as which of the following?

explain: Copyleft requires derivative works to carry the same freedoms and license terms. Proprietary and per-seat models restrict use, and public domain imposes no such condition.
q: A developer distributes modified software under a license requiring derivative works to be released under the same open terms. This licensing concept is known as which of the following?

explain: With COTS the buyer cannot fix code directly and depends on the vendors secure development and patching, making vendor evaluation essential. Both COTS and custom code need ongoing vulnerability management.
options: COTS eliminates the need for contracts
The vendor controls patching and code quality, so due diligence on vendor security practices is essential
q: When acquiring commercial off-the-shelf software instead of building custom software, what is the MOST important security trade-off to evaluate?

explain: Jailbreaking strips platform protections and sandbox guarantees while plaintext storage leaves secrets readable to other processes or forensic access. Jailbreaking weakens, not improves, enforcement, and shared preferences are not automatically encrypted.
options: Plaintext storage exposes secrets if the device or its storage is accessed
Jailbreaking removes OS protections that guard app data
q: A mobile banking app stores its API key and session tokens in plaintext in shared preferences on a jailbroken device. Which risks combine to make this MOST dangerous? (Choose two.)

explain: Rate limiting and throttling cap attempt frequency, blunting credential stuffing and brute force. Key size does not limit attempts, and removing logs or downgrading transport worsens security.
q: An API allows unlimited login attempts, enabling credential stuffing against user accounts. Which control MOST directly mitigates this?

explain: OAuth issues scoped, revocable tokens for delegated access without sharing passwords. Shared static keys lack scoping and revocation per user, and password sharing is never acceptable.
options: Static API key shared by all partners
Security through obscurity of the endpoint
Basic authentication with the user password
q: A partner integration needs delegated access to a users data without receiving the users password, with scoped and revocable permissions. Which mechanism BEST fits?

explain: API keys primarily identify the client application, whereas OAuth tokens carry delegated, scoped user consent. OAuth tokens do expire, and API keys are not user passwords.
options: API keys identify the calling application, while OAuth tokens represent delegated user authorization with scope
They are identical in all respects
API keys are always user-specific passwords
q: What is the PRIMARY difference between an API key and an OAuth token at the usage level?

explain: Returning unneeded sensitive fields is excessive data exposure rooted in weak access control and response filtering. The fix is server-side authorization and returning only required fields.
options: Excessive data exposure through missing authorization and filtering
q: A REST API returns full customer records including fields the requesting client never needs and is not authorized to see. Which flaw is MOST present?

explain: Store vetting is a limited point-in-time check; vulnerabilities and malicious behavior via updates or server-side changes still occur. Developers retain responsibility for secure coding and testing.
options: Stores review no applications at all
Store vetting is limited and cannot guarantee absence of flaws or later malicious updates
Vetting replaces the need for a firewall
q: A mobile app relies solely on being reviewed by the app store to guarantee it contains no malicious or vulnerable code. Why is this reliance UNSOUND?

explain: Sandboxing isolates apps so a compromised app cannot freely read other apps data or exceed its permissions. It does not guarantee flawless code or automatic traffic encryption.
options: It prevents the user from installing apps
It isolates each apps data and limits access to other apps and system resources
It guarantees apps are free of vulnerabilities
It encrypts all network traffic automatically
q: What security benefit does mobile operating system app sandboxing provide?

explain: Jailbreaking disables code signing and sandbox protections the OS relies on, sharply increasing malware risk. It voids rather than improves support and does not add encryption.
options: Removal of built-in OS protections, increasing malware and data exposure risk
q: A user jailbreaks a phone to install unsigned apps. What is the PRIMARY security consequence?

explain: A covert channel transfers information through means not intended for communication, such as resource timing or load, bypassing policy. Overt channels are authorized communication paths.
q: Two processes communicate by modulating shared resource usage, such as CPU load, to pass information in violation of the security policy. This is an example of which of the following?

explain: Allowing external entities in XML parsers lets attackers read files and trigger server requests; disabling DTD external entities is the fix. The other options describe unrelated session, timing, and database concepts.
options: XML external entity processing enabled by an insecure parser configuration
q: A web services endpoint accepts XML input and an attacker includes an external entity definition that reads a local file. Which class of flaw should developers prevent through parser configuration?

explain: Server-side enforcement on every request is authoritative because clients can be modified or bypassed. Hiding UI elements, client checks, or firewall rules alone cannot enforce object-level authorization.
options: On the server for every request
q: A security architect must decide where to enforce authorization for a web application used by both browsers and mobile clients. Where should enforcement occur to be authoritative?

explain: Internal services must still authenticate and authorize each other; trusting the network perimeter fails once an attacker is inside. Shared accounts and fail-open behavior compound the problem.
options: Never trust, always verify service identity on each request
q: A distributed applications microservices communicate without authenticating each other, trusting the internal network. An attacker who gains a foothold exploits this trust. Which design principle was violated?

explain: SameSite restricts when cookies are sent on cross-site requests, reducing CSRF. It does not address injection, memory corruption, or server-side request forgery.
q: An e-commerce site sets the SameSite attribute on its session cookie. What attack does this PRIMARILY help mitigate?

explain: Regenerating the session ID at authentication prevents fixation and pre-auth ID reuse. Longer timeouts, removing Secure, and URL-based IDs all increase session risk.
options: Store the session ID in the URL
Regenerate a new session ID after authentication
q: After successful login, an application keeps using the same session ID that existed before authentication. What is the BEST corrective action?

explain: Branch protection plus mandatory peer-reviewed pull requests restore controlled, attributable change. Shared accounts destroy accountability and deleting history destroys the audit trail.
options: Protect the main branch so direct commits are blocked
Require pull requests with peer review before merging
Disable commit history to save space
Share one developer account for all commits
q: A team discovers developers have been committing directly to the main branch of a payment application with no review. Which TWO changes BEST restore secure change control? (Choose two.)

explain: Threat modeling analyzes data flows and trust boundaries during design to find threats early and plan mitigations. Fuzzing tests inputs at runtime, signing proves origin, and acceptance validates delivery.
q: During design, a team maps data flows, trust boundaries, and attacker entry points for a new claims portal. Which activity are they performing?

explain: Fuzzing crashes point to code defects fixed by correcting the parser and validating input; a WAF cannot repair memory handling. Suppressing logs or faster restarts hide rather than fix the flaw.
options: By hiding the crash from logs
By fixing the parsing code and adding input length and format checks
q: A fuzzing tool sends malformed and random inputs to an applications parser and observes a crash indicating a memory flaw. At which level is this finding BEST addressed?

explain: Level 5 Optimizing centers on continuous, data-driven process improvement. Heroics characterize Level 1, basic documentation Level 2 and 3, and measurement is embraced, not eliminated.
q: An organization at CMMI Level 5 focuses on which activity?
A team is onboarding a new third-party JavaScript library into a production web application. Which TWO actions BEST reduce third-party component risk before deployment? (Choose two.)
options: Deploy the library first and assess it after the next incident
Review the library license obligations and confirm they are compatible with distribution plans
Assume a popular library is safe and skip review
Verify the component version against known vulnerability databases and check for a patched release
explain: Checking components against vulnerability data and confirming license compatibility are core due diligence for third-party software. Popularity is not assurance of safety, and assessing only after an incident leaves known flaws exposed in production.

Software assurance is the justified confidence that software is trustworthy, achieved through secure practices across the lifecycle. No process guarantees zero failures, and insurance or a single test is not assurance.
options: Confidence that software functions as intended and is free from exploitable vulnerabilities, built in throughout development
A guarantee that software will never fail
Insurance purchased to cover breach costs
q: Which statement BEST describes software assurance?

explain: Virtual patching shields known flaws at the WAF or RASP layer when code cannot change, buying time for replacement. Publishing code, removing logs, or widening rights increase risk.
options: Virtual patching with a WAF or RASP rules targeting its known flaws
q: A legacy application cannot be patched and must remain online for six months. Which compensating approach at the application layer BEST reduces exploitation risk?

explain: Automated SCA gating in CI/CD blocks critical vulnerable components before release consistently. Annual manual scans, memory, and post-breach checks all allow long exposure windows.
options: Scan dependencies once a year manually
Scan only after a breach occurs
Run SCA in the pipeline and fail the build on critical findings with no approved exception
Rely on developers to remember advisories
q: A development team wants to ensure a vulnerable dependency never reaches production again. Which pipeline design BEST achieves this?

explain: Defense in depth requires each service to enforce authorization because requests may bypass the gateway via internal paths or misconfiguration. Gateway logging exists, and API authorization remains essential.
options: Direct or internal calls bypassing the gateway reach unprotected APIs
q: An API gateway enforces authentication, but individual APIs skip their own authorization checks, trusting the gateway. Why is this dangerous?

explain: Forged cross-site requests ride the victims authenticated session; anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies defeat them. The scenario involves no injected query, stored script, or server-fetched URL.
options: XSS stored, countered by output encoding alone
CSRF, countered by anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies
SQL injection, countered by prepared statements
q: A user reports that after clicking a link in an email, a transfer was made from her logged-in banking session without her intent. Which attack MOST likely occurred and which control counters it?

explain: Concurrent unsynchronized operations are a race condition; atomic transactions and locking ensure only one withdrawal succeeds. The other pairs address memory, injection, and session flaws not present here.
options: Buffer overflow, fixed by bounds checking
Fixation, fixed by regenerating session IDs
Race condition, fixed by atomic transactions and proper locking
q: Two users submit requests to withdraw the last funds from a shared account at the same instant and both succeed, overdrawing it. Which flaw and fix pair is CORRECT?

explain: A gated secure SDLC with test evidence plus an SBOM with remediation performance concretely demonstrates maturity. Marketing spend and office decor provide no security assurance.
options: The color scheme of the vendors office
The size of the vendors marketing budget
An SBOM and vulnerability remediation timelines for components
Documented SDLC with security gates and recent independent test results
q: A SaaS vendor asks which TWO pieces of evidence BEST demonstrate secure development maturity during acquisition due diligence? (Choose two.)
